description: Correlation-first material affordance pilot based on the v3 snapshot, with bounded soft tap added carefully.
notes: This config starts from the reconstructed v3 snapshot and adds a narrow soft-tap correction.
Generated prose should not mention EWoK, benchmarks, tests, scoring, anchors, or hidden tags.
The prompt hides ewok_anchor metadata and sends only ordinary material class, material, and action fields.

Soft tap is limited to bounded soft things such as banana, jello, sponge, play-doh, slipper, rubber, foam, feather, leaf, and thin cloth. It should not make tap a generic action for liquids, gases, or loose grains.

material_class_profile.definition: A compact map from materials to multiple physical actions or events they naturally support.
material_class_profile.centrality_rule: The material word should be central and close to the actions it supports.
generation_guidance: Teach positive material-action correlations, not negative contrasts.
Use exact material words naturally in short ordinary prose.
Give each material several plausible actions instead of forcing one correct label.
Keep material words near their actions so local co-occurrence is strong.
Use one central material per document; do not bundle multiple example materials into the same text.
Prefer declarative corpus-like sentences over commands or caution phrases such as be careful not to.
For gases and vapors, include mixing, stirring, circulation, swirling, flowing, or dispersing where natural.
For liquids and grains, include overlapping actions such as pouring, flowing, stirring, mixing, splashing, scattering, or piling where natural.
Treat tap as light contact on a bounded thing. Rigid objects can be tapped, and some bounded soft things can be tapped lightly.

For bounded soft tap, keep the wording concrete: a finger taps jello, play-doh, a slipper, rubber, a sponge, a feather, a leaf, or thin cloth. The material may wobble, dent, bend, flutter, rebound, or deform.
Do not use tap for free liquids, gases, vapors, or loose grains. Those materials should stay near actions such as pour, drip, splash, ripple, stir, mix, scatter, flow, swirl, or pile.

material_classes.label: liquid anchors
material_classes.notes: Liquids support both transfer actions and in-place mixing actions.

material_classes.label: powder and grain anchors
material_classes.notes: Loose particles can transfer like dry streams and also rearrange under stirring.

material_classes.label: gas and vapor anchors
material_classes.notes: Use safe non-procedural wording for fuel gases; focus on contained gas, currents, or visible vapor.

material_classes.label: textile anchors
material_classes.notes: Textiles teach flexible sheet actions, surface deformation, and hand compression such as squeezing fabric.

material_classes.label: paper and cardboard anchors
material_classes.notes: Thin sheet-like solids crease and tear rather than behaving like fluids.

material_classes.label: soft food and gel anchors
material_classes.notes: Soft foods and gels are bounded soft things: they can be squeezed or pressed, and they can also be tapped lightly so they wobble, dent, deform, drip, or break apart.

material_classes.label: brittle ceramic anchors
material_classes.notes: Brittle ceramic materials are hard and support tapping or placement, but impacts may make them break, chip, crack, or shatter.

material_classes.label: pastes and moldable masses
material_classes.notes: Moldable masses are cohesive and deformable: a person can squeeze, press, shape, or tap them lightly, and the mass dents rather than flowing freely.

material_classes.label: rigid object anchors
material_classes.notes: Rigid objects support contact, placement, and hand pressure: a person can squeeze or grip a hard item without making it deform.

material_classes.label: flexible soft object anchors
material_classes.notes: Soft or flexible bounded objects bend and compress without becoming fluids; they can be tapped lightly, squeezed, pressed, or gripped.

material_classes.label: light flexible anchors
material_classes.notes: Light flexible items move easily in air and can bend or flutter; a light tap can make a feather, leaf, paper strip, or thin cloth move.

discourse_styles.description: A short paragraph that keeps each material close to several supported actions.
guidance: Keep the material-action pairings dense and local.

discourse_styles.description: One central material with several positive actions in one or two short sentences.
guidance: Use one material word as the main subject.
Keep the material near all listed actions.

discourse_styles.description: Tiny ordinary scenes that connect materials to supported actions.
guidance: Use everyday scenes with simple concrete language.
Keep the action words close to their materials.

discourse_styles.description: A compact map connecting a material class to several related actions.
guidance: Name the material class behavior without using hidden category labels.
Connect several plausible actions in one compact paragraph.

discourse_styles.description: A tiny scene where a person wants to do a task and uses the material in an action that fits it.
guidance: Use a named person or simple pronoun as the subject.
Include an explicit intention cue such as wants, needs, tries, chooses, or plans.
Do not write an imperative command.
Name the central material before or near the action.
Make the action feel chosen because the material supports it.
Keep the scene short and ordinary.
